slides.label: Title
slides.narration: Open with the transition from construction to deduction. Chapter 1 showed what compass and straightedge can build; this chapter asks what we can prove about those constructions. Euclid organized geometry around five postulates that govern lines, circles, right angles, and parallel lines. Orient students to printed pages 20 through 45.

slides.label: Lecture Route
slides.narration: Preview the five themes. Students should leave understanding congruence as a rigorous test for sameness, the parallel postulate as the axiom that distinguishes Euclidean geometry, area as something that can be proved equal by dissection, the Pythagorean theorem as a consequence of these ideas, and Thales theorem as a bridge between lines and circles.

slides.label: Five Postulates
slides.narration: Present the five postulates as the foundation. The first four are about local constructions; the fifth, the parallel postulate, is global and controversial. Emphasize that the entire structure of Euclidean geometry rests on accepting all five, and changing the fifth produces non-Euclidean geometries in Chapter 8.

slides.label: Congruence
slides.narration: Explain congruence through the SAS, ASA, and SSS criteria. Two figures are congruent when there is a rigid motion mapping one onto the other. In practice, matching a specific combination of sides and angles suffices to guarantee a unique triangle, and the three criteria cover the cases where this guarantee holds.

slides.label: Pythagorean Theorem
slides.narration: Show the Pythagorean theorem through area dissection. The classical proof rearranges two copies of the right triangle to fill a large square in two different ways, revealing that the area of the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the areas of the squares on the two legs.

slides.label: Thales Theorem
slides.narration: Introduce Thales theorem: an angle inscribed in a semicircle is always a right angle. Prove it by drawing the radius to the inscribed point and using the isosceles triangle property. This result connects circles to right angles and was already used in Chapter 1 for the square-root construction.

slides.label: Inscribed Angle Theorem
slides.narration: Present the inscribed angle theorem as a generalization of Thales: the inscribed angle is always half the central angle subtending the same arc. This powerful result links arc measure to angle measure and will reappear when projective geometry uses cross-ratios in Chapter 5.

slides.label: Regular Pentagon
slides.narration: Walk through the construction of a regular pentagon. The key is the golden ratio: dividing a segment so that the whole is to the longer part as the longer part is to the shorter. Once you can construct the golden ratio, the pentagon follows by marking five equally-spaced points on a circle.

slides.label: Recap
slides.narration: Summarize the chapter by connecting the five postulates, congruence, area dissection, and circle theorems into a coherent deductive system. Every result proved here rests on the postulates, and the parallel postulate in particular will be questioned when we reach non-Euclidean geometry in Chapter 8.
